newsitem.title: USA: Chicago Fed sees need to watch financial services.
newsitem.headline: Chicago Fed sees need to watch financial services.

text.p: - Participants at a three-day Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago conference found a need to watch but not yet regulate the fast-growing array of financial services made possible by new technology.

"We don't know enough about these new services to decide whether we should regulate them or how to regulate them," a Fed official told Reuters at the Chicago Fed's Conference on Bank Structure and Competition.
The conference focused on the impact of new technology on banking and financial services.
Chicago Fed President Michael Moskow told an audience of 500 bankers, banking experts and regulators "the prudent banker will realize both the possibilities and pitfalls of technology."

Like other Fed officials who addressed the conference -- Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, Governor Susan Phillips and Boston Fed President Cathy Minehan -- Moskow said technology-driven changes in financial services bear watching.
"The goal of this approach is to align the incentives of banks with those of regulators," Moskow said, referring to the Fed's role as a regulator of the U.S. banking sector.

The common theme in most papers presented at the conference dealt with the fact new financial technologies, such as Internet transactions or stored-value cards, are too recent to permit a definitive evaluation of the risks.
William Hunter, director of research at the Chicago Fed, said "banks are in good shape right now ... but technology is one of the big wild cards facing the industry."

"It will determine the future structure of the industry in terms of products we use. It's a very timely point to look forward about what we can bring in terms of future strategies into the next millennium," Hunter said.
MasterCard International President Jerry McElhatton warned that the "old lines between banking, insurance and financial markets are blurring. Non-banks are in your markets."
"I believe that the financial services business is facing a fundamental upheaval in structure and delivery," he said.

Arthur Kennickel, a senior economist at the Fed Board, presented a paper that showed banks' most valuable customers in the high-income group also are most likely to use technology for their decisions. Overall, however, Kennickell noted "banks have not been very successful at becoming a major source of financial information."

Brian Smith, a partner at Mayer, Brown and Platt, warned that the emergence of smart and digital money may lead to the "banking industry being virtually ... bypassed by the electronic currency process."
One risk tied to electronic money is that it may be created by non-regulated entities whose failure would have far-reaching consequences both for the public and within the payments sytem.

Moskow, commenting on third-party payments, said the dominant view among experts seems to be that "this role should be restricted to regulated depository institutions in order to maintain the integrity of the payments systems."
The conference also noted one important advantage of technology, the possible disappearance of paper checks, which could save the U.S economy as much as $100 billion a year in clearing costs.
Also listed among the advantages of new financial services technology were "data mining" or increased information about customers, easier mortgage lending and broader credit availability.
